title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
purpose: Opens the book with its author's dedication, occasion and title, then begins the doctrinal exposition by defining faith, its first level, the seven obligations and twelve practices, and the distinction between faith and Islam.

points.text: The author states that he composed the book at the repeated request of a senior figure of the dawa, to gather into one place what lies scattered through the books of the saints and their learned callers — the paired and authoritative books, the brief compositions on Sharia matters, and expansive treatments of juristic paths and legal opinions — so that their contents would be made more accessible.

The author names the book إسعاف الطالب في جميع المطالب ('The Student's Aid in All Demands') and dates the start of composition to the seventh of Rajab al-Asabb in the year 1051 of the Prophetic migration.

The author writes from within the Tayyibi Ismaili tradition, invoking the Prophet, 'Ali, Fatima al-Batul, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, the pure Imams, and the caller of his own age, the dai Jafar ibn Sulayman and his successor the dai Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, in service to the Imam al-Tayyib.

The author disclaims personal credit: whatever in the work is correct derives from the substance of his patron the caller and his successor, while whatever is a slip or error comes from his own shortness of reach.
Reporting from 'some of the noble books', the author states that faith has eight levels (مراتب).

The first of the eight levels of faith is charity (الإحسان) toward parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the nearby neighbor, the companion at one's side, the traveler, and those whom one's faith obligates one to care for — a level the author says is established in the Book of God.

The quoted source asserts that whoever undertakes the worship of God and the call of the People of the House without knowledge and without action cannot rightly bear the name of faith, and holds no bond with God nor covenant or honor with His guardian, having departed from faith.
The author announces that he will next treat the distinction between faith (iman) and Islam — what each encompasses — and what lies beyond them.

Quoting the fourth of the Mustansiriyya Councils (the Councils of Exposition and Wisdom), the author reports that the Imams of religion are seven, recurring in the world as the days of the week recur until the rising of the Qa'im, while twelve proofs (hujjas) are spread throughout the world — and this constitutes knowledge of the sum of the limits (hudud) of the testimony.

The author distinguishes knowing the limits of the testimony from fulfilling the rights owed to those limits: the latter consists of upholding seven obligations of religion and twelve practices incumbent upon the God-fearing, mirroring the seven Imams and twelve proofs.
The seven obligations of religion are guardianship (walaya), purity (tahara), prayer (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting (sawm), pilgrimage (hajj), and struggle (jihad).

The twelve practices are honoring parents, maintaining kinship ties, protecting the neighbor, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, truthfulness in one's home, good conduct with one's spouse, kindness to dependents, spreading the greeting of peace, feeding others, keeping the bond among the brethren, and visiting the sick — and the author states these twelve are not obligatory upon women.

The author cites 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts that the Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects and this community will divide into seventy-three, of which one is in the Garden and the rest in the Fire.
